title: Efficiency experts call a basic hand motion a ‘therblig’: ‘Gilbreth’ almost backwards

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still of a worker’s hands at a wooden bin of small metal parts, with a large clock dial labelled Gilbreth beside it.
cover.credit: Frank B. Gilbreth (presented by James S. Perkins) · Public domain

body: Frank Gilbreth started out in 1885 as a bricklayer’s helper and noticed how differently bricklayers went about the same job, which set him hunting for ‘the one best way’ to do any task. Working with his wife Lillian, also an industrial engineer, he used a motion picture camera calibrated in fractions of minutes to time even the smallest movements workers made. According to a 1968 account by Claude George, Gilbreth reduced every motion of the hand to combinations of **17 basic motions**, such as grasp, transport loaded and hold, and named them **therbligs**.

slides.alt: Black-and-white film from a Gilbreth motion study: a worker’s hands take a tag, reach into a wooden bin of small metal parts and slide out a drawer, while a large clock dial labelled Gilbreth ticks beside the bin.
slides.caption: From efficiency expert Frank Gilbreth’s motion-study films of 1910–1924: a clock in the shot, which the film calls a micro-chronometer, times each reach and grasp at a parts bin.
slides.credit: Frank B. Gilbreth (presented by James S. Perkins) · Public domain · excerpt

left.label: Frederick Taylor
left.text: His symbol was the stopwatch. The aim: cut the time a job takes.

right.label: The Gilbreths
right.text: Cut the motions a job needs. Fewer motions also meant less tiring work.

slides.explanation: The stopwatch was the symbol of Frederick Taylor, with whom the Gilbreths fell out. The caddy, the vertical scaffold and the weapon drills were Gilbreth’s.

slides.question: Besides wasting time, what did the Gilbreths say needless motions caused?
slides.explanation: Some motions were not just unnecessary but tiring, so they also changed tools, parts placement and bench and seat heights: groundwork for ergonomics.
